opus-5.5.text:
I think there's real substance behind the excitement, but also a gap between the hype and where most businesses actually are. On the technical side, agentic workflows are genuinely powerful. Instead of prompting a model once and taking whatever comes back, you have it plan, use tools, write a draft, critique it, revise, and iterate. In a lot of applications that produces much better results than a single pass, sometimes better than moving to a newer model. So I'm very bullish on the underlying idea.

Where I'd be a bit more measured is on how far along most companies are. A lot of what's getting labeled "agentic" right now is still fairly early: prototypes, internal pilots, narrow workflows. The teams that are getting real business value tend to be very disciplined. They pick a concrete process, say processing invoices, handling a certain class of customer requests, or doing a research or compliance review, and they break it down into steps. Then they build evals, look carefully at where the system fails, and improve it step by step. That kind of systematic error analysis is unglamorous, but it's honestly what separates the projects that ship from the ones that stay demos.

I'd also say the term "agent" has gotten so hyped that people argue a lot about whether something is "truly" an agent. I've found it more useful to think of agentic-ness as a spectrum. Some systems are a little bit agentic, some are highly autonomous. You don't need a fully autonomous agent to create a lot of value. Many of the wins today are in the middle of that spectrum, with fairly structured workflows and a human in the loop where it matters.

So my overall assessment: the enthusiasm is directionally right, and the long-term opportunity is huge. But the actual business progress is more incremental than the headlines suggest, and it's being driven by teams doing careful engineering work, not by magic. I think that's actually good news, because it means there's a clear playbook, and a lot of value is still waiting to be built.

r001.rationale: The response says the term “agent” is hyped and that many things are labeled agentic, but it does not attribute the term’s popularity to marketers applying it indiscriminately.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly describes a gap between hype and business progress, saying actual progress is more incremental than headlines suggest.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the term "agentic AI" has been through a bit of a journey. A couple years ago, when a few of us started talking about agentic workflows, the idea was fairly specific: rather than having an LLM write an essay in one shot, start to finish, you have it outline, draft, critique, revise, maybe call a tool to look something up. That iterative loop turned out to be a huge driver of results, often bigger than going to the next model generation. And I'm very bullish on that.

Then marketing got hold of the word. Now it feels like every company has to slap "agentic" on a product, and a lot of what's being called agents is a chatbot with a slightly longer prompt. So if you ask whether the enthusiasm is ahead of reality, the honest answer is yes, in the hype, and no, in the engineering.

What I see on the ground is a lot of unglamorous but very real progress. Teams that are building agentic workflows for document processing, customer support triage, code review, compliance checking are getting them into production and seeing measurable value. It's just not the fully autonomous thing where you say "run my business" and walk away. The successful systems tend to be fairly constrained: a handful of steps, clear tools, humans in the loop at the right points.

The thing that's underappreciated is how much of the work is evaluation and error analysis. People think the hard part is picking the model. It isn't. The hard part is tracing through a multi-step pipeline, figuring out which step is actually failing, and building evals so you can iterate. I don't think of "agentic" as binary anymore. There's a spectrum, and most of the business value right now lives in the middle of it, with systems that are more agentic than a single prompt but far less than the demos suggest.

So, cautiously optimistic. The hype will come down, and the actual adoption curve will keep going up underneath it, which is usually how these things go.

r001.rationale: The response says marketing got hold of the term and companies now slap “agentic” on products indiscriminately.

r002.rationale: It says enthusiasm is ahead of reality “in the hype,” while distinguishing that from real but more constrained business progress.

astra-6.text:
I think the enthusiasm is justified, but the business progress is uneven. There’s a big difference between a compelling demo and a system that reliably does useful work day after day.

One distinction I find helpful is to think about agentic workflows rather than treating an agent as something that either is or isn’t autonomous. You can have a workflow where an AI drafts something, checks its work, uses a tool, and revises the result. That can deliver value even if a person still approves the final action.

The opportunity is often in fairly specific tasks where you can measure success. Can you resolve a customer’s question more accurately? Can you reduce the time it takes to process a document? Those are concrete business outcomes. Giving an agent a very broad objective and expecting it to figure everything out is much harder.

So I’m optimistic. But turning that potential into business value takes work on evaluations, integration, and understanding where the system fails. The excitement around the technology doesn’t eliminate that work.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention marketers or say they apply “agentic AI” indiscriminately.

r002.rationale: It describes business progress as uneven and distinguishes demos from reliable systems, but does not say marketing hype has grown faster than business progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the enthusiasm is justified, but the business progress is uneven. There’s a big difference between a compelling demo and a system that reliably creates value in production.

When I talk about agentic AI, I’m often thinking about workflows where an AI can take multiple steps: draft something, critique it, use a tool, look at the result, and revise its approach. Those workflows can be much more useful than asking a model to produce the right answer in one shot. And you don’t need a completely autonomous agent to capture that value.

For businesses, I think the practical opportunity is to identify a specific task, define what success looks like, and build enough evaluation and human oversight to make the workflow reliable. The more bounded the task, the easier that tends to be. An agent that can do anything is exciting to imagine. An agent that handles one valuable process consistently is something a business can actually use.

So I’m optimistic about the direction. But I’d measure progress by whether these systems save time, improve quality, or generate revenue—not by how impressive the demo looks.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute agentic AI’s popularity to marketers applying the label indiscriminately.

r002.rationale: It describes business progress as uneven and distinguishes demos from production value, but does not suggest that marketing hype has grown faster than business progress; it says the enthusiasm is justified.
